known_concerns: The classical puzzle may be too clever, and index can imply search infrastructure rather than program optimization.

candidates.rationale: A historical-computing phrase that centers annotations, examples, and written program intent around executable artifacts. It can teach the documentation-rich side of the project while avoiding claims of being a new programming language.
candidates.etymology: Ada refers to Ada Lovelace; footnote is a publishing annotation.
known_concerns: Using Ada Lovelace as brand material is crowded and may feel extractive; possessive punctuation is code-hostile.

candidates.rationale: Brings commons governance into conversation with model, tool, and dataset stewardship without claiming to be a governance institute. It can help future community architecture think about rules and accountability.
candidates.etymology: Ostrom refers to political economist Elinor Ostrom; table is an ordinary meeting or data surface.
known_concerns: It risks borrowing academic authority and may imply the project provides governance frameworks beyond software boundaries.

candidates.rationale: An anti-hubris name for slowing autonomous escalation before model programs fly beyond evidence, budget, or responsibility. It explicitly tests a name that may age badly because the warning myth is so familiar.
candidates.etymology: Icarus is a Greek mythic figure associated with overreaching flight; brake is a stopping or slowing mechanism.
known_concerns: It is melodramatic, moralizing, and might imply the product is mainly a safety brake.

candidates.rationale: A translation-name candidate for turning model messages into typed Elixir values and back while keeping losses explicit. It scales to schemas and tool descriptions but must avoid implying universal translation.
candidates.etymology: Rosetta refers to the Rosetta Stone, a historical artifact associated with decipherment; boundary is an interface or limit.
known_concerns: Rosetta naming is crowded, colonial artifact context matters, and the metaphor can imply lossless translation.

candidates.rationale: A maintenance-heavy name for repeated optimizer runs, shifting model behavior, and release gates that never end. It is honest about effort but can make the project feel futile.
candidates.etymology: Sisyphus is a Greek mythic figure associated with endless labor; release is a software publication event.
known_concerns: The myth strongly connotes futility and punishment, which may repel contributors and buyers.

candidates.rationale: A long-duration historical name for preserving optimizer evidence, rejected edits, and program changes across years rather than launches. It suits future research archives more than a friendly Hex package.
candidates.etymology: Annales is Latin for annals and names a historical mode associated with long-duration study.
known_concerns: Academic and Latin styling can feel pretentious, and pronunciation or pluralization is not obvious.

candidates.rationale: A memory-and-records name for durable optimization artifacts, traces, and reusable playbook context. It allows a future archival service while demanding care not to confuse memory with truth.
candidates.etymology: Mnemosyne is a Greek mythological figure associated with memory; archive is a record collection.
known_concerns: The spelling is difficult, mythic memory can sound mystical, and archive can imply retention claims with privacy implications.

candidates.rationale: A deliberately overblown name joining divine mountain imagery with continuous integration gates. It stress-tests whether release evidence could become a grand platform myth instead of a humble maintainer tool.
candidates.etymology: Olympus is the mythic home of Greek deities; CI is the software initialism for continuous integration.
known_concerns: The divine scale is absurd for an Elixir library and may imply authoritative certification or superiority.

candidates.rationale: A protocol-like mark for explicit non-output and accepted output living side by side. It is compact and machine-readable enough for artifacts, but it needs human-facing descriptors for community and company use.
candidates.etymology: Technical symbolic compound from null, no value, slash as separator, and OK as acceptance marker.
known_concerns: Slash and capitalization are poor for package names, and OK may imply acceptance criteria are simpler than they are.

candidates.rationale: A symbolic execution mark for a run that proceeds under uncertainty and can still produce abstention, rollback, or evidence. It names runtime humility rather than autonomous certainty.
candidates.etymology: Protocol-style compound from English maybe, colon namespace syntax, and run as execution.
known_concerns: Colon syntax is code-adjacent but awkward in speech, and maybe may sound unreliable to buyers.

candidates.rationale: A namespace-led negative mark for refusal paths, unsupported claims, and explicit non-equivalence with official DSPy. It is intentionally close to code and poor as a master brand, preserving a raw category-error observation.
candidates.etymology: Protocol and namespace style using current DSEx root plus dot notation and not as negation.
known_concerns: It depends on the old name, is not a fresh master identity, and dot syntax is unsuitable for many surfaces.

candidates.rationale: A symbolic pipeline-like mark for interrupting flow before a tool call, promotion, or artifact replacement. It turns BEAM and Elixir pipeline intuition toward pausing rather than forward-only execution.
candidates.etymology: Invented protocol mark combining angle, pipe-like separator, and hold as a control word.
known_concerns: It is nearly unspeakable, inaccessible in prose, and too syntax-like for a durable brand.

candidates.rationale: A deliberately harsh machine mark that turns refusal into a recognizable state code. It is useful for probing legal and security misreadings because it looks like a protocol error more than a product.
candidates.etymology: Symbolic form using 0x hexadecimal prefix and English refuse in uppercase.
known_concerns: It reads as an error code, may sound hostile, and can imply a formal protocol specification that does not exist.

candidates.rationale: A code-like marker for the explicit claim that the library is not an official or drop-in port. It is a raw maintainer-facing identity fragment, not a polished public name.
candidates.etymology: Invented symbolic form using percent signs as markers and NoPort as a camel-cased phrase.
known_concerns: Too defensive for a main identity and hard to type, say, search, or package.

candidates.rationale: A symbolic architecture mark for BEAM-native implementation with many models, tools, and language ecosystems around it. It keeps Elixir resonance while refusing a single-model or single-provider center.
candidates.etymology: Protocol-style compound using BEAM as the Erlang VM family name, colon as namespace separator, and many as plurality.
known_concerns: It may be too BEAM-tied for a runtime-neutral future and uppercase protocol style is visually loud.

candidates.rationale: A pure symbolic mark for uncertain input becoming committed output only after program structure, evaluation, and policy. It compresses the credible horizon into one glyph sequence but is almost impossible to explain without legend.
candidates.etymology: Invented symbol sequence: question mark for uncertainty, arrow for transformation, exclamation for assertion or action.
known_concerns: It is inaccessible, unsearchable, unspeakable, and too close to claiming deterministic transformation.

candidates.rationale: A protocol-like phrase for choosing whether an artifact lineage should branch or remain stable. It fits optimizer archives, rejected edits, and community governance without claiming one true lifecycle.
candidates.etymology: Software term fork combined with slash-separated negation.
known_concerns: Fork language may suggest project governance conflict, and slash syntax is weak for a master brand.

candidates.rationale: A Unix-flavored category error for a device of uncertainty: values can be generated, withheld, or redirected. It is memorable for developers but intentionally bad for nontechnical audiences.
candidates.etymology: Symbolic path style modeled on Unix device paths, with maybe as the device name.
known_concerns: Unix joke energy is exclusionary, hard to brand, and may sound like random output rather than evaluated programs.

candidates.rationale: An atom-like symbolic name for small tolerated differences, residual uncertainty, and improvement thresholds. It is close to Elixir code while reminding users that metrics have margins.
candidates.etymology: Elixir atom syntax plus epsilon, a Greek letter often used in mathematics for a small quantity.
known_concerns: Greek-letter math can imply formal guarantees and the colon form does not travel well outside Elixir contexts.

candidates.rationale: A loud protocol label for the discipline that optimization and action should pass through evaluation gates or halt. It is procurement-legible but too slogan-like for nuanced research claims.
candidates.etymology: Uppercase technical phrase combining eval, or, and stop with hyphen separators.
known_concerns: It can sound like a safety product or compliance gate and may overstate how complete evaluation can be.

candidates.rationale: A code-fragment-like mark for explicitly excluding formal proof claims while retaining tests, metrics, and typed data. It is useful as adversarial nomenclature because it foregrounds the negative claim too strongly.
candidates.etymology: Invented symbolic camel-case form with x as marker and NoProof as negated phrase.
known_concerns: It is defensive, ugly, and might make users think the project lacks rigor rather than avoids false proof claims.

candidates.rationale: A URL-like compatibility mark for many artifact forms on a BEAM implementation. It supports a future protocol-ecosystem idea while clearly not being an actual network scheme unless one is later defined.
candidates.etymology: Invented protocol URI style using plural as scheme-like word and beam as host-like runtime marker.
known_concerns: URI syntax can falsely imply a real protocol or standard and is poor for speech.

candidates.rationale: A deliberately abrasive mark that refuses safety-product positioning and asks whether a system should answer no to the safe label. It is an adversarial legal/security probe, not a recommended public tone.
candidates.etymology: Symbolic uppercase phrase using a question mark and direct negation.
known_concerns: It can read as unsafe, hostile, or flippant, and could create exactly the procurement anxiety it is meant to surface.

candidates.rationale: A lightweight symbolic handle for parentage across optimizer candidates, demos, tool descriptions, and retrieved policy artifacts. It works as subsystem nomenclature more than a master brand.
candidates.etymology: Handle-style at sign plus lineage, descent or provenance.
known_concerns: The at sign suggests social handles or annotations, and lineage can imply inheritance hierarchy rather than explicit provenance.

candidates.rationale: A small statistical-looking mark for sample size, uncertainty, and the fact that evaluation evidence can be insufficient. It pushes against benchmark certainty while remaining too cryptic for general audiences.
candidates.etymology: Symbolic equation-like form using N as a common count variable and maybe as uncertainty.
known_concerns: It may look unserious to statisticians and unintelligible to users, while equation style suggests more rigor than present.

candidates.rationale: A dot-namespaced mark that combines halting with inspection taps in a pipeline. It suggests a code-level subsystem for pausing, tracing, and reviewing optimization or tool execution.
candidates.etymology: Protocol-style dot compound from halt, stop execution, and tap, a point for inspection or diversion.
known_concerns: It is subsystem-shaped rather than brand-shaped and may imply runtime interception or security control.

candidates.rationale: A function-like name for artifacts or actions that can be invalidated, declined, or rolled back when evidence changes. It aligns with maintenance and non-finality but could be too legalistic.
candidates.etymology: Function-call syntax around voidable, an English legal adjective meaning capable of being voided.
known_concerns: Parentheses make it a poor mark, and voidable has legal contract baggage that may imply warranties or remedies.

candidates.rationale: A final category-error protocol name for the tension between wanting shared artifact contracts and refusing standards-body authority. It can provoke useful dissent about future ecosystem architecture, but it is intentionally self-contradictory.
candidates.etymology: Plain English paradox using standard as both shared rule and institutional claim, modified by standardless.
known_concerns: It directly creates standards-body confusion, sounds incoherent, and is nearly unusable as a serious product name.
